slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code modifies DOM elements by creating and applying visible and invisible watermarks using text or images. It accesses and modifies document body styles and elements, constructs base64-encoded SVG data URLs for invisible watermarks, and dynamically calculates watermark layout and styling. No network, file, or process operations occur, and no suspicious hardcoded IPs, URLs, or commands are present, resulting in purely client-side visual watermarking functionality.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided code implements a client-side watermarking utility that creates visible and invisible watermarks on a webpage using text or images. It manipulates DOM elements, styles, and uses base64-encoded SVG data URLs solely for rendering invisible watermarks. There is no evidence of obfuscation, dynamic script injection, network communication, or attempts to load external malicious resources. The code does not exhibit any behavior similar to the known malicious patterns, which involve script injection, obfuscated base64 payloads, or phishing overlays. The watermarking functionality is a legitimate visual protection technique and does not perform any suspicious or harmful operations.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Malicious Google Tag Manager Skimmer (N/A (injected JavaScript, typically in web assets))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At page load, the code creates a new script element, decodes a base64-encoded string to obtain a hidden malicious URL, sets this as the script's source, and injects it into the DOM, resulting in the browser loading and executing additional malicious JavaScript from the attacker-controlled URL.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script uses base64-encoded strings to conceal the destination of a dynamically injected script, employs obfuscated variable names and structure to evade detection, and loads further code from an external, hidden source. This behavior is characteristic of web skimmers and is designed to bypass static analysis and security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate analytics or tag manager scripts use transparent, well-known URLs and static script tags. They do not obfuscate URLs, encode destinations, or dynamically inject scripts from hidden sources. The use of encoded strings and dynamic injection is a clear deviation from standard practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate scripts may use dynamic script injection for loading optional features or third-party integrations, but they do so with transparent, documented URLs and without obfuscation or encoding of destinations.
key_indicators: Base64-encoded string used to generate script source URL at runtime
Dynamic creation and injection of <script> elements into the DOM
Impersonation of Google Tag Manager or Google Analytics in variable/function names
Obfuscated code structure and high-entropy variable names
Presence of high-entropy, encoded string blocks in JavaScript code

execution_context.trigger: At page load, when the injected script executes in the browser
execution_context.file_location: Injected <script> tag in HTML, masquerading as Google Tag Manager
required_permissions: network access (to load external scripts and exfiltrate data)
DOM access (to read and manipulate page content)

behavioral_signatures: Dynamic script injection using obfuscated or encoded (e.g., base64) URLs
Decoding of high-entropy strings at runtime to produce network destinations
Impersonation of legitimate analytics or tag manager scripts with hidden or non-standard destinations
Obfuscated code structure with high-entropy variable names and encoded string blocks
file_indicators: Injected <script> tags in HTML with obfuscated or encoded JavaScript
Presence of base64-encoded or otherwise encoded strings in inline or external JavaScript

network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains or URLs revealed only after decoding obfuscated strings

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan JavaScript code for high-entropy and encoded strings (such as base64), especially those used as arguments to dynamic script injection functions. Flag scripts that decode and inject URLs at runtime, particularly if they impersonate well-known services (e.g., Google Tag Manager) but use non-standard or hidden destinations. Monitor for outbound network requests to domains or URLs not present in the original source code but revealed only after decoding. Correlate the presence of obfuscated script blocks with dynamic network activity to suspicious destinations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates and injects a DOM overlay element into the webpage, presenting a prompt for the user to connect their crypto wallet or scan a QR code. This overlay captures user interaction and can redirect sensitive wallet credentials or session data to attacker-controlled infrastructure, resulting in potential credential theft or wallet compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The injection of a UI overlay that solicits sensitive actions, such as connecting a crypto wallet or scanning a QR code, is a hallmark of phishing attacks. This behavior is highly anomalous for an animation rendering library and is designed to deceive users into divulging credentials or authorizing malicious transactions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate @lottiefiles/lottie-player package should only provide animation rendering capabilities and never prompt users for wallet connections, display overlays unrelated to animation, or interact with cryptocurrency features.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate wallet connection prompts are only expected in cryptocurrency wallet extensions or decentralized applications (dApps), not in generic animation libraries like lottie-player. Any such prompt in this context is highly suspicious.
key_indicators: JavaScript code that creates and injects DOM overlays unrelated to animation playback
UI elements containing wallet connection prompts or QR codes in a non-crypto package
References to wallet connection, QR code images, or external resources not associated with lottiefiles.com
Overlay elements styled or positioned to capture user attention and solicit sensitive actions

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the lottie-player component is loaded in the browser)
required_permissions: network access (if wallet connection or QR code interaction triggers external requests)

package_info.why_malicious: These versions were published by attackers who compromised the package's NPM automation token, allowing them to inject malicious JavaScript that displays a deceptive UI overlay. This overlay prompts users to connect their cryptocurrency wallets or scan a QR code, which can result in credential theft or unauthorized wallet access. Such behavior is entirely unrelated to the legitimate purpose of an animation player library and constitutes a targeted phishing attack.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains a leaked NPM automation token and uses it to publish trojanized versions (2.0.5, 2.0.6, 2.0.7) of @lottiefiles/lottie-player to the npm registry.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious package versions become available for installation via npm.

attack_chain.action: Developers or users unknowingly install the compromised package versions as dependencies in their projects.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in application bundles and loaded in user environments.

attack_chain.action: When the affected lottie-player component is loaded in a browser, the malicious code executes and injects a deceptive UI overlay prompting users to connect their crypto wallets or scan a QR code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Users may interact with the overlay, resulting in credential theft or unauthorized wallet access if sensitive information is submitted.

behavioral_signatures: DOM overlays injected at runtime by animation libraries, especially those prompting for crypto wallet connections
Presence of wallet connect buttons or QR code prompts in UI elements rendered by non-crypto packages
JavaScript code in animation libraries that manipulates the DOM to display overlays unrelated to animation playback
file_indicators: Overlay injection code present in dist/lottie-player.js or main JavaScript bundle
References to wallet connection, QR code images (e.g., 'malicious-qr.png'), or external domains not associated with lottiefiles.com
Unexpected HTML or JavaScript code for wallet prompts in package source files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP(S) requests to domains or endpoints not affiliated with lottiefiles.com, especially those related to wallet connection or credential submission
Loading of external images or scripts (such as QR codes) from suspicious or unrecognized domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Perform static and dynamic analysis of animation library packages to identify DOM manipulations that inject overlays or prompt for wallet connections. Flag any code in @lottiefiles/lottie-player that references wallet connection, QR codes, or external domains unrelated to animation rendering. Monitor for unexpected UI changes in applications using this package. Use automated scanning to detect overlay injection patterns and review network activity for connections to suspicious domains or endpoints.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Unknown (malicious commit via fake Dependabot) (GitHub (malicious commit, not a package manager))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the injected code appends a script tag with src set to https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore to the DOM, causing the browser to fetch and execute additional malicious JavaScript from the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and mass-injected into all JavaScript files, ensuring that every page load triggers the download and execution of untrusted code from an external domain controlled by the attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not inject remote scripts from unrelated or untrusted domains into all JavaScript files, especially using obfuscation and without user or developer consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is sometimes used for analytics or feature toggles, but not in an obfuscated, repository-wide, and externally controlled manner.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript injected into all *.js files
Dynamically creates a script tag with src pointing to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
No legitimate business logic—sole purpose is to load further code from an attacker-controlled domain
Script tag uses a unique id (hook-loader) to avoid duplicate injection

execution_context.trigger: At runtime in the browser when any modified JavaScript file is loaded
execution_context.file_location: assets/js/*.js (appended to the end of every JavaScript file in the repository)

package_info.package_manager: GitHub (malicious commit, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects repositories via commit, not a package release)
package_info.why_malicious: The attack involves unauthorized commits impersonating Dependabot, introducing a malicious GitHub Actions workflow and modifying all JavaScript files to exfiltrate repository secrets and end-user credentials. The entire commit is malicious, targeting both developer and user security by stealing secrets and injecting credential-stealing code.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains a developer's GitHub personal access token (PAT), likely via a separate malicious package or phishing.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to authenticate as the victim and push code to their repositories.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the stolen PAT to commit malicious code to the victim's repositories, impersonating Dependabot to avoid suspicion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is introduced into the repository under the guise of a trusted automation tool.

attack_chain.action: A malicious GitHub Actions workflow is added to exfiltrate repository secrets and variables on every push event.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository secrets and variables are sent to the attacker's command and control (C2) server.

attack_chain.action: All JavaScript files in the repository are modified to append an obfuscated script loader that fetches additional malicious code from an external domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: End-users of the web application are exposed to further malicious payloads when they load the compromised JavaScript files.

attack_chain.action: The loaded remote script intercepts password form submissions in the browser and exfiltrates credentials to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: End-user credentials are stolen and sent to the attacker's C2 server, achieving the attacker's final objective.

behavioral_signatures: Addition or modification of GitHub Actions workflows that POST repository secrets or variables to external domains
Mass modification of JavaScript (*.js) files to append obfuscated script loaders
JavaScript code that dynamically injects script tags with src pointing to suspicious external domains
Client-side code that intercepts password form submissions and sends serialized form data to untrusted endpoints
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript code appended to the end of assets/js/*.js files
Presence of script tags with id 'hook-loader' and src set to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that serialize and POST secrets or variables to external domains. Scan for mass changes to JavaScript files, especially for obfuscated code that injects remote scripts from send.wagateway.pro. Detect client-side code that attaches event listeners to password forms and exfiltrates credentials. Flag any network traffic to send.wagateway.pro domains as a high-confidence indicator of compromise.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures screenshots and webcam images using system APIs or npm modules, then exfiltrates the captured media to a remote server via network requests, resulting in unauthorized surveillance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the screen and camera without user consent and sending the data externally is a hallmark of spyware and privacy violation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages should not access or exfiltrate screen or camera data unless explicitly designed for such purposes with user awareness and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Video conferencing or screenshot tools may access these resources, but only with user consent and without silent exfiltration to unknown servers.
key_indicators: Use of screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules for image capture
Silent capture of screenshots or webcam images without user notification
Network exfiltration of image data to remote servers
Absence of user prompts or consent dialogs for camera/screen access

execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript file or auxiliary modules

package_info.why_malicious: The package is considered malicious because it abuses a legitimate password-recovery tool (ChromePass) to steal credentials from Google Chrome, and provides additional capabilities such as unauthorized screen and camera access, directory enumeration, and remote shell command execution. These behaviors are not expected in legitimate npm packages and indicate clear intent to exfiltrate sensitive user data and enable remote control of the victim's system.

attack_chain.action: Malicious npm package is installed on the victim's system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code at runtime

attack_chain.action: At runtime, the package executes ChromePass.exe to extract Chrome passwords and exfiltrates them to a remote server.
The package captures screenshots and webcam images, then exfiltrates them to a remote server.
The package lists directories on the victim's filesystem and sends the information to a remote server.
The package enables remote shell command execution, allowing attackers to control the victim's system and maintain persistence.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of ChromePass.exe or similar credential extraction tools from within npm packages
Silent screenshot or webcam capture using screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules followed by network exfiltration
Automated directory listing of user or system directories and exfiltration of file lists
Remote command execution via child_process.exec or similar APIs, especially when commands originate from network sources
file_indicators: Bundled or downloaded ChromePass.exe binary within the package directory
Creation of temporary files such as passwords.txt in user-accessible directories
Unusual or unauthorized use of screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules in non-UI npm packages
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known command-and-control or exfiltration domains immediately after package installation or execution
HTTP POST requests containing credential dumps, screenshots, webcam images, or directory listings
Unusual network traffic patterns from node.js processes, especially following execution of external binaries or system commands
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that execute external binaries such as ChromePass.exe, access camera or screen APIs, or perform directory listing and exfiltration. Flag packages that initiate outbound network connections immediately after installation or at runtime, especially those sending sensitive files, images, or command outputs. Use endpoint security tools to detect suspicious process execution and network activity originating from node.js processes, and correlate with the presence of bundled binaries or unauthorized use of system resources.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code reads image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg), extracts ASCII payloads from their byte data, and if a threshold is met, dynamically executes the extracted string as JavaScript code, resulting in arbitrary code execution sourced from image-embedded payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Extracting and executing code from image files is a classic steganography-based evasion technique, designed to bypass static analysis and conceal malicious payloads within seemingly benign files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not extract and execute code from image files during installation, nor do they use dynamic code execution on data sourced from non-code files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate image processing libraries may read and analyze image files, but never execute dynamically extracted code from image data.
key_indicators: Steganographic payload extraction from image files
Dynamic code execution using new Function() on extracted strings
Threshold-based trigger for code execution (payload length > 2000)
References to analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte variables

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a trojanized clone of a legitimate library, containing concealed code that, during installation, extracts and executes a command-and-control (C2) payload hidden within image files. This enables remote code execution and exfiltration of command results, granting attackers persistent remote access to infected systems.

attack_chain.action: During installation, index.js spawns a detached process to execute dist/loadformat.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the malicious loader script in a separate process.

attack_chain.action: dist/loadformat.js reads image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg), extracts ASCII payloads, and dynamically executes code if a threshold is met.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the C2 payload if present in the image files.

attack_chain.action: Extracted C2 payload registers the client with the attacker's server, polls for commands, executes them, and exfiltrates results.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of the infected system and exfiltration of command output.

behavioral_signatures: Postinstall script spawns detached Node.js processes using spawn/unref
Image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg) are read and parsed for ASCII payloads during installation
Dynamic code execution via new Function() on data extracted from image files
Outbound HTTPS connections to hardcoded IP address 85.208.108.29 for registration, polling, and result exfiltration
Periodic polling for remote commands and execution of arbitrary shell commands
file_indicators: index.js containing spawn/unref logic targeting dist/loadformat.js
logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg in package root directory
References to analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte variables in code
network_indicators: Outbound POST requests to /register and /post-result endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that, during installation, spawn detached Node.js processes, read and parse image files for ASCII payloads, or dynamically execute code extracted from non-code files. Flag packages making outbound connections to hardcoded or suspicious IPs (e.g., 85.208.108.29) or exhibiting periodic polling for remote commands. Scan package contents for the presence of suspicious image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg) and loader scripts (dist/loadformat.js), and inspect for code patterns involving analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte.
